summary: Gives guidelines for designing new URL schemes, helping authors define how a new kind of address should look and behave. This is an informational memo, and it was replaced by RFC 4395.

eli5.summary: This is a how-to guide for inventing a new kind of address that everyone's browser can understand.

questions: how to define a new url scheme
subtitle: A how-to guide for defining the syntax and semantics of new URL schemes.

tldr.problem: As the web grows, people want to define new URL schemes for different kinds of resources, but without clear guidelines this leads to incompatible and hard-to-implement designs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides six key criteria: new schemes must be syntactically compatible with existing URI syntax, have well-defined semantics, demonstrate genuine utility, address security considerations, avoid names starting with 'UR', and consider whether relative URLs and proxy gateways are practical.
tldr.outcome: Authors defining new URL schemes can follow these guidelines to ensure interoperability, deployability and compatibility with the existing URL ecosystem. This RFC was replaced by RFC 4395.

today: RFC 2718 was replaced by RFC 4395, which updated the guidelines for URL scheme registration and provides refined design criteria for modern web schemes.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Locator (URL) is a text string representing a location for a resource on the Internet. URLs consist of a scheme (like http: or ftp:), a colon, and a scheme-specific part (like //example.com/path). Many URL schemes already exist, and new ones are regularly proposed.

RFC 2718 provides guidelines for those defining new URL schemes, helping ensure they work well with existing schemes and software. The registration process for new schemes is defined separately in RFC 2717. These guidelines help avoid schemes that are poorly designed, redundant, or incompatible with existing infrastructure.
sections.eli5: URLs are addresses like http://example.com. The guidelines help people invent new addresses that work well with browsers and websites.

sections.title: Syntactic Compatibility
sections.content:
New URL schemes should follow the generic URI syntax from RFC 2396 when appropriate. If a scheme does not share fragment syntax (the part after hash) with others, content with embedded links cannot be moved between schemes without rewriting. Similarly, if relative URL syntax (like ../) is not shared, sets of documents cannot be moved together. If the slash path separator or double-slash authority syntax is not shared, it becomes difficult to serve identical content via multiple schemes or reorganize directory hierarchies.

Double slashes should only appear after the scheme when the scheme-specific part has a hierarchical structure with a naming authority (the host name). Many URL schemes incorrectly use double slashes as mere decoration. The scheme definition must specify what parts of RFC 2396 syntax apply, and if some characters have different meanings, this must be clearly documented.
sections.eli5: New URL schemes should use the same rules for things like slashes and fragments that other URLs use, so you can move links and content between them without breaking everything.

sections.title: Well-Defined Semantics
sections.content:
The resource being located by the URL must have clear, unambiguous semantics. When a new scheme maps from an existing protocol or namespace (like the ftp: scheme mapping from the FTP protocol), the mapping must be complete and describe how all characters are encoded, which modifiers are included or excluded, and exactly how legal values of the base standard are represented.

For schemes associated with network protocols, the specification must describe how URLs translate into protocol actions in sufficient detail to make access unambiguous and identify any required configuration. For non-protocol schemes (like cid: for content identifiers), the specification must define the notation and mapping. For schemes that do not locate data resources (like mailto: for email addresses), the properties of names in the new space must be clearly defined. Character encoding should follow UTF-8 plus percent-encoding unless there is compelling reason otherwise.
sections.eli5: The new URL type needs clear rules about what it points to, how to find it, and what computers can do with it—no guessing allowed.

sections.title: Demonstrated Utility
sections.content:
New URL schemes must have demonstrated utility. Creating URL scheme support requires special code in browsers, proxies and servers, so schemes should either point to things that cannot be referred to another way, or provide significant advantages over existing methods like proxy gateways.

One practical way to demonstrate utility is via a gateway that serves resources from the new scheme through HTTP, so clients can access them via standard browsers without native scheme support. Effective gateways need a single global resolution mechanism (or allow users to run their own), operations that map one-to-one to HTTP, well-defined types for returned objects, and working prototype code.
sections.eli5: Before inventing a new URL type, prove it is actually useful. There must be a real problem it solves better than what already exists.

sections.title: Security and Naming
sections.content:
Beyond security of the underlying mechanism, URL designers must consider normal usage scenarios. Can users be tricked into triggering the scheme without explicit request? Can URLs be forged to point to dangerous things while appearing valid? Are there identity mechanisms that need protection, like passwords in URLs? Will the scheme pass security information in the clear, which could expose credentials?

Additionally, any scheme name starting with 'U' and 'R' (implying 'universal', 'uniform' or 'unifying') will generate intense debate. Such proposals should either establish large consensus that the scheme is the only one of its type, or choose a different name.
sections.eli5: Think about bad actors. Can they trick people with fake URLs, steal passwords, or cause harm? Bad names also cause problems, so pick simple ones.
